newsitem.title: CHINA: FORECAST-China GDP seen up 10.5 pct in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-China GDP seen up 10.5 pct in 1997.

text.p: China's economic growth may accelerate next year, spurred partly by political factors, to hit 10.5 percent, the China Daily Business Weekly said on Sunday.

Gross Domestic Product in 1997 may reach 8,178 billion yuan ($985.3 billion), rising 10.5 percent compared with an anticipated 9.6-9.7 percent increase this year, the newspaper quoted Xu Hongyuan of the State Information Centre as saying.

The five-yearly Communist Party congress set for late in 1997 was expected to take some difficult decisions to eradicate the low economic efficiency and operational losses plaguing thousands of lumbering state enterprises, Xu said.
"These political factors, if the government makes use of them smoothly, will provide strong backing to national economic performance in 1997," the newspaper said, quoting Xu.
He forecast retail price inflation to speed up slightly to about 8.0 percent from an expected 7.0 percent this year.

Foreign trade was expected to make a strong recovery after exports slumped in the first few months of this year, especially as the government completes repayment of billions of dollars of export rebates to exporters.
He forecast exports to reach $171.5 billion in 1996, up by 14.1 percent compared with this year.
Xu urged a further cut in import tariffs next year.
However, Xu forecast a sharp increase in unemployment. In 1997, there could be as many as 8.0 million jobless, including workers left idle because of suspension of factory production.
The urban jobless rate could reach 8.0 percent next year if both surplus workers at factories and registered unemployed are included, Xu said.
China's official registered urban jobless rate was 2.98 percent at the end of September.
The government was likely to take measures to avoid any steep jump in foreign exchange reserves, which now totalled $98 billion, he said.
Failure to do so would add additional burdens to the People's Bank of China, the central bank, in extending credits in renminbi, the local currency, he said.
